## 🧩 The mystery

It is your very first day. Prof. Zola waves you toward an empty desk with a
laptop on it and says one thing:

> "Get set up. We start real work tomorrow."

Then she is gone.

Amina (that is you) sits down. No pipettes. No reagents. No bench. Just a
laptop and a blinking cursor. And a small, honest question: set up *what*,
exactly?

Here is the thing nobody tells you on day one. A wet-lab scientist does not
start an experiment by grabbing the first tube in sight. They set up their
bench first. Clean surface. Tips in the rack. Reagents labelled. Only then do
they start.

You are about to do the same. The only difference is that yours is a **dry lab**
bench, made of software instead of glassware. (Wet lab means the physical bench
with pipettes and reagents. Dry lab means the computational one.) Get it right
once, and every experiment in every module after this just works.

::: {.think}
Most bioinformatics tools are written for Unix, a family of operating systems
that includes Linux and macOS. Windows is not Unix.

So before you install a single tool, ask: does your computer even speak the
right language yet? **Yes? No? Not sure?** Hold that thought. We will sort it
out together, one small step at a time.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A gentle word before we begin

If you have ever opened a "beginner" tutorial and met a wall of cryptic
commands on line one, welcome. You are among friends, and that is *not*
happening here.

This module is the least glamorous part of bioinformatics. Nobody grows up
dreaming of installing a package manager. But it quietly decides whether
everything *after* it goes smoothly or turns into a week of mysterious errors.
Getting it right once saves you a genuinely enormous amount of pain later.

Three honest things to set expectations:

- **This is a guided tour, not the whole map.** These tutorials get you moving
  and show you the lay of the land. Real comfort takes *your* effort too:
  reading the official docs, experimenting, looking things up when stuck. We
  point you to good sources along the way.
- **You learn this by doing, not reading.** Type the commands yourself. Hitting
  an error is not failure, it *is* the work. Every bioinformatician you admire
  has squinted at a baffling error message today.
- **Go at your own pace.** No points for speed, nobody is timing you. When a
  step misbehaves, take a breath. The **⚠️ Verify** and **🧰 Troubleshooting**
  notes exist precisely because you are not the first person to trip there.

One small step at a time, and you will be fine. Let us build your bench.
:::

## What you will have built by the end

By the end of this module you will have:

1. A working **Unix command-line environment**: **Ubuntu Linux via WSL2** on
   Windows, or the built-in **Terminal** on macOS.
2. **Conda** (via Miniforge) installed as your package and environment manager.
3. The **Bioconda** and **conda-forge** channels configured, so you can install
   thousands of bioinformatics tools with one command.
4. Your **first isolated environment** with a couple of real tools in it, plus
   the skill to *reproduce* that environment from a file.

This is the foundation for every other module in the series. Take your time. A
clean setup now saves hours later.

## 💬 Why a whole "bench" and not just one tool?

::: {.story}
Picture a chemistry bench. The reason a scientist keeps reagents in labelled,
separate bottles (and not all sloshed into one bucket) is simple: if project A
uses one buffer and project B needs another, mixing them ruins both.

Software is the same. Tools have versions, and versions clash. Conda gives you
labelled bottles for software, called **environments**, so project A's tools
never break project B's. That is the whole reason we bother with all this
setup.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Who needs which part: pick your track
This module has **two setup tracks** that then merge:

- **On Windows?** Do **Part A (Windows)**, install Ubuntu with WSL2, then
  continue to Part B and C.
- **On a Mac?** Do **Part A (macOS)**, prepare Terminal and developer tools,
  then continue to Part B and C.
- **On native Linux?** You already have a shell. Skim Part A, then start at
  [Part B](#part-b-install-conda-miniforge).

Parts **B (Conda)** and **C (channels plus first environment)** are the **same
for everyone**.
:::

### Before you start (prerequisites)

**Windows:**

- **Windows 10 (version 2004 or newer) or Windows 11**, with administrator
  rights.

**macOS:**

- A reasonably recent version of **macOS**. Note whether your Mac has an
  **Apple Silicon** chip (M-series) or an **Intel** chip. It matters later
  (see the Apple Silicon callout in Part C). Check via the
  **Apple menu → About This Mac**.

**Everyone:**

- A stable internet connection and a few GB of free disk space.
- Comfort with copy-pasting commands and reading the output carefully.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify: versions change
Every version number below (Ubuntu release, Miniforge, tool versions) is an
**example at the time of writing**. Installation methods for WSL and Conda have
changed before and may change again after my knowledge cutoff. When a step
matters, I point you to the official source to confirm. If a command behaves
differently than described, check the official docs first. Do not assume the
tutorial is still current.
:::

## Part A (Windows): Install Linux (Ubuntu) with WSL2

Think of this part as arriving in a new country. Your Windows machine speaks
one language, and bioinformatics tools speak Unix. Instead of emigrating (wiping
Windows), you are opening a small, fully functional Ubuntu embassy inside
Windows. Same building, second language, both work.

::: {.callout-tip}
**On a Mac?** Skip this section and jump to
[Part A (macOS)](#part-a-macos-prepare-your-mac).
:::

### A.1 What is WSL, and why do we need it?

Most bioinformatics tools are written for **Unix-like systems (Linux/macOS)**.
Rather than dual-booting or wiping Windows, **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**
lets you run a real Ubuntu Linux environment *inside* Windows. "WSL2" is the
current architecture, which runs a genuine Linux kernel and is what you want for
bioinformatics.

You get a real Linux terminal, real Linux tools, and your Windows files are still
accessible. This is the standard, well-supported way for Windows users to do
bioinformatics.

### A.2 Check your Windows version

WSL's simple one-command install needs a recent Windows. To check:

- Press `Windows key + R`, type `winver`, press Enter.
- You want **Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or higher**, or **Windows 11**.

::: {.callout-note}
If you are on an older build, update Windows first (Settings → Windows Update).
Older manual WSL installation paths exist but are more error-prone. Updating is
the smoother route.
:::

### A.3 Install WSL + Ubuntu

Open **PowerShell as Administrator**:

- Click Start, type `PowerShell`, right-click **Windows PowerShell**, choose
  **Run as administrator**.

Then run:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

On a supported, up-to-date Windows this single command enables the required
features and installs the **default Ubuntu** distribution.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify
`wsl --install` and its behavior are defined by Microsoft and have changed across
Windows updates. The authoritative, current instructions live in Microsoft's
official WSL documentation. If `wsl --install` errors out, search Microsoft's
official "Install WSL" documentation for your exact Windows version rather than
trusting any single fixed command.
:::

**Reboot when prompted.** After rebooting, Ubuntu often finishes its setup
automatically and opens a terminal window.

#### Choosing a specific Ubuntu version (optional)

To see available distributions:

```powershell
wsl --list --online
```

To install a specific one (example, confirm the exact name from the list above):

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu-22.04
```

::: {.callout-tip}
For teaching, I suggest sticking with a recent **LTS** ("Long-Term Support")
Ubuntu release, because tutorials and tool support target LTS versions. Which
release is "current LTS" changes over time. Check ubuntu.com if unsure.
:::

### A.4 First launch: create your Linux user

The first time Ubuntu starts, it asks you to create a **UNIX username and
password**. Notes:

- This user is **separate** from your Windows account.
- When typing the password, **nothing appears on screen** (no dots, no stars).
  That is normal Linux behavior, not a frozen terminal. Type it and press Enter.
- Remember this password: you will need it for `sudo` (administrator) commands.

::: {.callout-important}
## Security: never paste secrets you do not understand
Only run commands you understand or that come from a trusted source. Never paste
a command from a random website that asks for your password without knowing what
it does.
:::

### A.5 Update the package lists

Inside your new Ubuntu terminal, update the software catalog and upgrade installed
packages:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
```

- `sudo` = run as administrator (it will ask for the Linux password from A.4).
- `apt` is Ubuntu's system package manager (different from Conda, which we install
  next).
- `-y` auto-confirms the upgrade.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check: did it work?
When it finishes without red `E:` error lines, you are good. You can confirm your
Ubuntu version with:

```bash
lsb_release -a
```
:::

### A.6 Where are my files? (Windows ↔ Linux)

This trips up almost everyone at first. Think of it as two rooms connected by a
narrow doorway:

- Your **Windows** drives are visible inside Linux under `/mnt/`. For example your
  Windows `C:\` drive is at `/mnt/c/`, so your Downloads folder is roughly
  `/mnt/c/Users/<YourWindowsName>/Downloads`.
- Your **Linux home** directory is `~` (which is `/home/<your-linux-user>`).
- From Windows, you can browse Linux files by opening File Explorer and typing
  `\\wsl$\` (or `\\wsl.localhost\`) in the address bar.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Performance tip that matters a lot
Keep your **analysis project files inside the Linux filesystem** (for example in
`~` or a subfolder), **not** under `/mnt/c/...`. Reading and writing many files
across the Windows/Linux boundary is noticeably slower and can cause
file-permission headaches. Treat `/mnt/c` as a place to *copy files in and out*,
not to run pipelines from.
:::

### A.7 (Optional but recommended) Nicer tools

- **Windows Terminal**: a modern terminal app that makes working with WSL much
  more pleasant (tabs, better fonts). Available from the Microsoft Store.
- **VS Code + the "WSL" extension**: lets you edit files and run the terminal
  seamlessly inside your Linux environment from a graphical editor. From your
  Ubuntu terminal you can typically launch it in the current folder with:

  ```bash
  code .
  ```

  (The first time, VS Code installs a small helper into WSL.)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 🧰 Troubleshooting Part A
- **`wsl --install` says it is not a recognized command** → your Windows is likely
  too old, or you are not in PowerShell. Update Windows; use PowerShell (not the
  legacy Command Prompt) as Administrator.
- **Virtualization error / WSL2 will not start** → virtualization may be disabled
  in your BIOS/UEFI, or the "Virtual Machine Platform" Windows feature is not
  enabled. This is hardware/firmware specific; consult Microsoft's official WSL
  troubleshooting page for your machine. I cannot give a one-size-fits-all fix
  here, and I will not guess your BIOS layout.
- **Forgot your Linux password** → it can be reset, but the procedure differs by
  setup; look up the current official method rather than an old forum command.
:::

## Part A (macOS): Prepare your Mac

::: {.callout-tip}
**On Windows?** This section is not for you. Use
[Part A (Windows)](#part-a-windows-install-linux-ubuntu-with-wsl2) instead.
:::

### A.1 (Mac) Good news: you already have Unix

macOS is built on a Unix foundation, so, unlike Windows, you **do not need WSL**.
You already have a real Unix shell. There are just a few things to set up so
bioinformatics tools install cleanly.

Your bench is half built already. You just need to lay out a few tools.

### A.2 (Mac) Open the Terminal

- Press `Cmd + Space`, type `Terminal`, press Enter.
- Modern macOS uses **`zsh`** as the default shell (older versions used `bash`).
  Everything in this series works in either; occasionally you will see a note where
  they differ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check: which shell am I in?
```bash
echo $SHELL
```
This prints something ending in `zsh` or `bash`.
:::

### A.3 (Mac) Install the Command Line Developer Tools

These provide essentials like `git`, `curl`, and compilers that many tools expect:

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

A dialog box will pop up. Click **Install** and accept the license. If it says
the tools are *already installed*, you are good.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify
Apple's developer-tools installation flow changes between macOS releases. If the
command above does not behave as described, check Apple's current guidance for
installing the Command Line Tools for your macOS version.
:::

### A.4 (Mac) Know your chip: Apple Silicon vs Intel

This is the one Mac-specific thing that genuinely affects bioinformatics, so note
it now:

- **Apple Silicon** = M-series chips (the architecture is called `arm64`).
- **Intel** Macs use the `x86_64` architecture.

Check with either the **Apple menu → About This Mac**, or in the Terminal:

```bash
uname -m
```

- `arm64` → Apple Silicon
- `x86_64` → Intel

**Why it matters:** historically, some bioinformatics packages on Bioconda were
built for Intel Macs (`osx-64`) but **not** yet for Apple Silicon (`osx-arm64`).
We handle this in [Part C's Apple Silicon callout](#apple-silicon-note). For now,
just know which chip you have.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify: this situation improves over time
The availability of native Apple-Silicon (`osx-arm64`) builds for bioinformatics
packages has been **increasing over time**, so what is true today may be better by
the time you read this. Do not assume a tool is unavailable on Apple Silicon
without checking the current Bioconda package listings.
:::

#### (Optional) Rosetta 2: running Intel software on Apple Silicon

If you are on Apple Silicon and later need to run `x86_64`-only software, macOS uses
a translation layer called **Rosetta 2**. You can install it with:

```bash
softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify
`--agree-to-license` auto-accepts Apple's software license agreement on your
behalf. Only run it if you are comfortable doing so; otherwise omit that flag and
accept the license interactively. Confirm the current command in Apple's
documentation. Intel-Mac users do **not** need Rosetta.
:::

### A.5 (Mac) A note on Homebrew (optional)

Many Mac users install **Homebrew**, a general-purpose macOS package manager. It is
genuinely useful for everyday tools, **but for this series we use Conda** for
bioinformatics software, because Conda environments are how we keep projects
reproducible and isolated. You do **not** need Homebrew to follow these tutorials.
If you already have it, that is fine; if not, skip it for now.

### A.6 (Mac) File locations

Unlike WSL, there is no Windows/Linux boundary to worry about. It is all one native
filesystem. Your home directory is `~` (that is, `/Users/<your-username>`). Keep your
analysis projects anywhere convenient in your home folder.

::: {.callout-warning}
## 🧰 Troubleshooting Part A (Mac)
- **`xcode-select --install` says "command line tools are already installed"** →
  that is fine, nothing to do.
- **A tool later fails to install on Apple Silicon** → see the
  [Apple Silicon callout in Part C](#apple-silicon-note); it is almost always an
  architecture (`osx-arm64` vs `osx-64`) issue, not a mistake on your part.
:::

---

## Part B: Install Conda (Miniforge)

You now have a bench (a Unix shell). Next you need a way to fetch and organise
tools without chaos. That is Conda.

::: {.callout-note}
✅ From here on, the steps are the **same for Windows (inside your Ubuntu/WSL
terminal) and macOS (in Terminal)** unless a callout says otherwise.
:::

### B.1 What is Conda, and why Miniforge?

**Conda** is a package and environment manager. It lets you:

- Install scientific software (and its dependencies) without `sudo`.
- Create **isolated environments** so Project A's tools do not break Project B's.

There are several ways to get Conda. This tutorial uses **Miniforge**, a minimal
installer that is community-maintained and defaults to the **conda-forge**
channel.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify: licensing has changed before
Historically people installed "Miniconda"/"Anaconda", which use Anaconda, Inc.'s
"defaults" channel. **Anaconda changed the terms of service** for using their
channels, and some organizational/commercial uses may require a paid license.
This is exactly the kind of thing that changes over time and that I cannot
authoritatively rule on for your situation. **Miniforge** sidesteps this by using
the community **conda-forge** channel by default, which is why it is recommended
here. If licensing matters for your institution, verify the *current* terms
yourself. I am not able to give you legal advice.
:::

Recent Miniforge installers also include **`mamba`**, a faster drop-in
alternative to the `conda` command. Where you see `conda install ...` below, you
can usually substitute `mamba install ...` for speed.

### B.2 Download and run the installer

The Miniforge project provides installers on its official GitHub releases page
(the `conda-forge/miniforge` repository). A commonly documented one-line download
that auto-detects your OS and CPU architecture is:

```bash
curl -L -O "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"
```

Then run the installer:

```bash
bash Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh
```

Follow the prompts:

- Press Enter / `q` to page through the license, then type `yes` to accept.
- Accept the default install location (usually `~/miniforge3`) unless you have a
  reason not to.
- When asked whether to run `conda init`, answering `yes` sets up your shell so
  `conda` is available in new terminals.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify
Download URLs, installer filenames, and available architectures are defined by the
Miniforge project and can change. If the `curl` command 404s, go to the official
`conda-forge/miniforge` GitHub releases page and copy the current installer link
for your system. Do not trust the exact URL above blindly. Confirm it resolves.
:::

### B.3 Activate conda in your shell

Close and reopen your terminal (or run the command the installer suggests, often
`source ~/.bashrc`). You should now see `(base)` at the start of your prompt,
indicating the base conda environment is active.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check: is conda working?
```bash
conda --version
```
This should print a version number. If instead you get "command not found", the
shell init step did not run. Reopen the terminal, and if it still fails, re-run
the installer's init step (look up the current `conda init` usage).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Stop `(base)` from auto-activating (optional preference)
Some people prefer conda *not* to auto-activate its base environment in every new
shell. If that is you:

```bash
conda config --set auto_activate_base false
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## macOS note
The `curl` one-liner in B.2 auto-detects macOS vs Linux and Intel vs Apple Silicon
via `$(uname)` and `$(uname -m)`, so the same commands work. You installed `curl`
already with the Command Line Tools in Part A (macOS). Apple-Silicon users: see the
[Apple Silicon callout in Part C](#apple-silicon-note) about package availability.
:::

---

## Part C: Configure channels and build your first environment

Conda is installed. The final step is to tell it *where* to find bioinformatics
software, and then build your very first environment. This is the moment the
bench actually gets its tools.

### C.1 What are "channels"?

Channels are the repositories Conda downloads packages from. For bioinformatics
the two that matter are:

- **conda-forge**: a huge community channel of general scientific software.
- **bioconda**: the channel specifically for bioinformatics tools
  (aligners, samtools, etc.). **Bioconda depends on conda-forge.**

Think of them as two supply catalogues your bench orders from.

### C.2 Configure the channels

The Bioconda project documents a specific channel setup. A widely used
configuration is:

```bash
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict
```

Because `--add` puts each new channel on top, the resulting priority order is
**conda-forge (highest) → bioconda → (whatever else)**, which is the order
Bioconda expects. `channel_priority strict` makes dependency resolution more
reliable and faster.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify: this is a "check the current docs" step
Bioconda's recommended channel configuration has been updated over time,
partly in response to the Anaconda "defaults" channel licensing changes mentioned
earlier. The three commands above reflect the common conda-forge-first pattern,
**but the officially recommended setup is exactly the kind of thing that changes**.
Before relying on this for real work, confirm the current recommended channel
configuration on the **official Bioconda documentation site**. If your later
`conda install` commands fail to find packages or complain about channels, an
out-of-date channel config is the first thing to check.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check your channel config
```bash
conda config --show channels
```
Confirm `conda-forge` is listed above `bioconda`.
:::

### Apple Silicon: when a Mac package "is not found" {#apple-silicon-note}

**Apple Silicon (M-series) users, read this before C.3.** Intel Mac, Windows,
and Linux users can skip to C.3.

Sometimes on Apple Silicon a `conda create`/`conda install` fails with a
`PackagesNotFoundError` for a bioinformatics tool. A common cause is that the tool
has an Intel-Mac build (`osx-64`) but not yet a native Apple-Silicon build
(`osx-arm64`). A widely used workaround is to create an **Intel (`osx-64`)
environment**, which then runs through **Rosetta 2** (installed in Part A):

```bash
# Create the env forcing the Intel package set:
CONDA_SUBDIR=osx-64 conda create -n bioinfo-intro fastqc samtools

# Activate it, then make future installs into THIS env also use osx-64:
conda activate bioinfo-intro
conda config --env --set subdir osx-64
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify: this is version- and tool-dependent
Two important caveats I want to be honest about:

1. **Native `osx-arm64` support keeps improving.** For many tools you may *not*
   need this workaround at all. Try the normal command in C.3 first, and only
   fall back to `osx-64` if you actually hit a "not found" error.
2. The `CONDA_SUBDIR` / `conda config --env --set subdir` approach reflects a
   commonly documented pattern, but the **exact mechanism can change between conda
   versions**. Confirm the current recommended approach in the official conda
   documentation before relying on it, and check the tool's Bioconda page to see
   whether an `osx-arm64` build now exists.
:::

### C.3 Create your first environment

**Never install project tools into `base`.** Instead, make a dedicated
environment. This is the labelled-bottle rule from the very start of the module,
now in practice. Let us create one called `bioinfo-intro` with two classic tools:

- **FastQC**: quality control reports for sequencing reads.
- **samtools**: a Swiss-army knife for reading/writing sequence alignment files.

```bash
conda create -n bioinfo-intro fastqc samtools
```

- `-n bioinfo-intro` names the environment.
- Conda will show a plan of packages to install; type `y` to proceed.

::: {.callout-tip}
Swap `conda` for `mamba` for a faster solve if Miniforge installed it:
`mamba create -n bioinfo-intro fastqc samtools`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify: pin versions for real projects
For a quick demo, installing "latest" is fine. For **reproducible** work you
should pin versions, for example `fastqc=<version>` and `samtools=<version>`. I am
deliberately *not* hard-coding version numbers here because whatever I write would
go stale. When you build a real analysis environment, record the exact versions
you used (see C.6).
:::

### C.4 Activate and use the environment

```bash
conda activate bioinfo-intro
```

Your prompt should now show `(bioinfo-intro)`. Confirm the tools are available:

```bash
fastqc --version
samtools --version
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check
Each command should print a version string. If you get "command not found", make
sure the environment is **activated** (you should see `(bioinfo-intro)` in your
prompt), not `(base)`.
:::

### C.5 Deactivate / switch environments

```bash
conda deactivate
```

This returns you to `base` (or no environment). Switching between projects is just
`conda activate <name>`. List all your environments any time with:

```bash
conda env list
```

## 🎉 What just happened?

::: {.insight}
Step back and see what you built. You did not just install two tools. You built a
sealed room, `bioinfo-intro`, put FastQC and samtools inside it, and can now open
and close that room at will with `conda activate` and `conda deactivate`.

Next project needs different tools? Build a different room. They never touch each
other. That isolation is the entire point, and it is why your future self will
never spend a week debugging "it worked yesterday."
:::

### C.6 Reproducibility: export and rebuild an environment

This is one of the most important habits in bioinformatics. **Your analysis is
only trustworthy if someone else (including future-you) can recreate the exact
software environment.**

Export the currently active environment to a file:

```bash
conda env export > environment.yml
```

This `environment.yml` records the channels and the exact package versions. To
recreate the environment somewhere else (another machine, a collaborator's
laptop):

```bash
conda env create -f environment.yml
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Two flavors of export
- `conda env export` captures everything, including exact builds. Most
  reproducible, but can be OS-specific.
- `conda env export --from-history` captures only the packages *you explicitly
  asked for*. More portable across operating systems, less exact.

For teaching/portability, `--from-history` is often nicer; for locking down a
production pipeline, the full export is safer. **Verify the exact flag behavior in
the current conda docs**, as export options have been refined over time.
:::

A minimal hand-written `environment.yml` looks like this (you can keep one of
these per module in an `env/` folder):

```{.yaml filename="env/bioinfo-intro.yml"}
name: bioinfo-intro
channels:
  - conda-forge
  - bioconda
dependencies:
  - fastqc
  - samtools
  # For real work, pin versions, e.g.:
  #   - samtools=1.XX      # <-- replace with a real, current version
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify
The `1.XX` above is a placeholder, **not a real version number**. I am not
asserting a specific samtools version exists. Look up the current version on the
tool's official page or with `conda search samtools` before pinning.
:::

### C.7 Cleaning up (optional)

To remove an environment you no longer need:

```bash
conda env remove -n bioinfo-intro
```

To reclaim disk space from cached downloads:

```bash
conda clean --all
```

## 🚧 The mistake almost everyone makes

::: {.mistake}
Day two arrives. You are excited. You install your next tool with a quick
`conda install <tool>` while `(base)` is showing in your prompt. It works. You
move on.

Weeks later, `base` is a tangled mess of clashing versions, and something breaks
for no visible reason. This is the number-one beginner trap: **installing tools
into `base`**.

`base` is the lobby, not an office. Keep it clean. Every project gets its own
named environment. Always.
:::

## 🧩 Mini challenge

::: {.challenge}
Prof. Zola drops by and says: "Build me a second environment called `align-demo`
with an aligner in it, and hand me a file I can use to rebuild it exactly."

Before you read on, sketch the commands in your head.

**Answer:** create the environment (verify the package name first with
`conda search`), activate it, then export it.

```bash
conda create -n align-demo bwa      # or bowtie2; confirm the name with conda search
conda activate align-demo
conda env export > env/align-demo.yml
```

Two tools, one file, fully reproducible. That is the whole habit in three lines.
:::

## Three quick questions

Not graded. Just checking yourself.

1. Should you install project tools into `base`, or into a named environment?
2. Which command saves an environment to a file you can rebuild it from?
3. On the channel priority order, should `conda-forge` sit above or below
   `bioconda`?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
A named environment (never `base`). `conda env export > environment.yml`.
`conda-forge` sits *above* `bioconda`, the order Bioconda expects.
:::

## 🎯 Key takeaway

::: {.takeaway}
Setting up your bench is not the boring bit before the real work. It *is* real
work. A Unix shell, Conda, configured channels, and isolated, reproducible
environments are the quiet foundation that makes every experiment after this one
just work. Build it once, carefully, and stop fighting your own tools forever.
:::

::: {.didyouknow}
Bioconda distributes thousands of bioinformatics packages and has been used to
install software for a huge share of published sequencing studies. The moment you
ran `conda config --add channels bioconda`, you plugged into the same supply line
that countless labs around the world rely on every day.
:::

## Where to go next

You have finished the setup module, the foundation the rest of the series builds
on. If parts of this felt fiddly, that is completely normal and not a sign you are
"not a computer person." Shells and package managers are genuinely unintuitive at
first, and become second nature only with repetition.

So the most useful thing you can do now is **practise**: create a few throwaway
environments, install tools, break them, delete them, rebuild them. Muscle memory
is the whole game. And remember these tutorials are a starting point, not the
finish line. Lean on the official docs for WSL, Conda, and Bioconda whenever you
want to go deeper.

::: {.callout-important}
## One more time on accuracy
If any command in this module did not behave as described, the most likely reasons
are (1) a version/OS difference, or (2) the tool changed after this was written.
Check the official documentation for **WSL (Microsoft)**, **Miniforge
(conda-forge)**, **Conda**, and **Bioconda**. Those are the authoritative sources,
and they supersede this tutorial whenever they disagree with it.
:::
